marble.name: The Water Cycle
marble.subject: Science
marble.description: Describe the water cycle, tracing water through evaporation, condensation, precipitation, surface runoff, and transpiration in plants, explaining how the sun drives the cycle
marble.prompt: If you watched rain falling outside and was asked where that water had been before it fell, could they trace its journey through the water cycle from the sea to the clouds to the rain and back?

cluster.summary: Your child is exploring how living things interact with their environment — learning about different habitats, simple food chains, and the difference between living, dead, and never-alive things.

misconceptions: Thinking the water cycle runs by itself without recognising the sun as the energy source driving evaporation.
Omitting transpiration, so plants are left out of the cycle.
Believing clouds are made of water vapour (invisible gas) rather than condensed liquid droplets.
Assuming human land use (deforestation, paving) has no effect on the water cycle, treating it as fixed.
representations: Labelled water-cycle diagram including transpiration and surface runoff
A followable water droplet travelling sea→vapour→cloud→rain→runoff→sea
Sun-as-engine annotation driving evaporation; gravity driving precipitation/runoff
Land-use comparison: forested vs paved catchment (transpiration and runoff differ)
authoredAnswer: The water is not gone — the sun's heat evaporated it into invisible water vapour in the air. It returns as rain when the vapour rises, cools and CONDENSES into cloud droplets that fall as precipitation. The sun drives evaporation and powers the whole cycle; plants add water vapour by transpiration. The same water is recycled — none is created or destroyed.
probe: Mini water cycle: put warm water in a clear bowl, cover with cling film, and rest an ice cube on top. The child first PREDICTS what will happen to the water level and whether the evaporated water is 'gone', and says why. Watching droplets form under the chilled film and drip back tests the 'the water disappears' idea a

wrongAnswers.wrong: The puddle water is gone — it dried up and disappeared.
wrongAnswers.revealedBy: Says the puddle water disappeared or was destroyed, naming no vapour.
wrongAnswers.fix: Reteach evaporation as a change of state, not destruction: the liquid became invisible vapour that is still there in the air.

wrongAnswers.wrong: Rain falls when the cloud gets too full and heavy with water.
wrongAnswers.revealedBy: Explains rain by clouds filling up rather than vapour cooling and condensing.
wrongAnswers.fix: Tie precipitation to cooling: rising vapour cools, condenses to droplets, which grow and fall — fullness isn't the trigger, cooling is.
Distinguish invisible vapour (the gas) from the visible cloud of tiny liquid droplets that forms when it condenses.
